Oil & gas · Ghana

Know what is on and beside your pipeline right of way

Gas and product pipelines in Ghana cross coastal towns, farmland, forest and mining country. AfriScan screens the whole corridor, counts structures by distance from the line, flags new excavations and cleared ground, and gives your right-of-way team a ranked list of segments to visit first. Satellite first, drone detail where the approvals allow, and a person reviews the results before they reach you.

Send your pipeline route See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

On the corridor, between patrols

Pipelines in Ghana cross coastal towns, farmland, forest and mining country. What appears on the right of way becomes a safety question first, and a compensation question later.

“Houses and kiosks are coming closer to the line.”

Towns grow along roads, and roads often run beside pipelines. New homes, shops, sheds and walls appear inside the corridor and just outside it, and each one is easier to discuss while it is new.

“Somebody has been digging near the pipe.”

Trenches for other services, borrow pits, building foundations and, in mining country, galamsey pits and washing sites can open close to a buried line. They show at the surface as fresh digging, spoil and cleared ground.

“The new line needs a route the land can carry.”

Before an investment decision, the options need comparing: how many structures each alignment passes, where settlement is growing, and which stretches cross rivers or steep ground.

“Our plant and depot have new neighbours.”

Settlement grows up to the fences of processing plants, booster stations and depots. The zones your engineers define around them need a current list of what stands inside.

The widths you measure against

Corridors acquired project by project

A summary of the public record as of 27 September 2026, for orientation. It is not legal advice; the sources are linked.

The width that matters is the width of your own corridor, which comes from the way its land was acquired. One onshore gas corridor, acquired under Ghana’s statutory wayleave and compulsory-acquisition regime, is described in a Supreme Court judgment of 15 December 2021 as “the right of way covering a distance of 111 Kilometres on a 35 metre corridor”.

So we measure to the width your corridor actually has: half the corridor either side of the centreline you send, or the boundary of the corridor polygon, with wider bands for planning and engagement. Tell us the instrument, wayleave or company standard the register should follow, and it is named in the report.

Downstream, petroleum products are regulated by the National Petroleum Authority under the NPA Act 2005 (Act 691); a new NPA Bill was before Parliament in September 2026.

A typical band set

  • The corridor itself, for example 17.5 m either side of a 35 m corridor
  • 50 m from the line
  • 100 m from the line
  • 200 m from the line, for planning

Several widths can be reported in one survey. Each structure carries its exact distance too, so any other width can be read from the register later.

Operating pipelines

A register of what stands on the corridor, then what changed

For an operating line, the first survey lists each structure the review confirms within the widths you set, with an ID, its distance to the centreline, its band, its chainage and its coordinates in WGS84 and the route’s UTM zone. Each 500 m segment is rated high, medium or low by the number of structures near the line, so the right-of-way team can plan its visits by segment rather than by kilometre post.

Re-surveys then flag what changed: new and removed structures, fresh excavations, trenches and spoil, cleared ground and new tracks across the corridor, each confirmed by a reviewer and shown before and after. A change notice after each survey says what changed and where, and settlement-growth trends show which stretches are filling up year by year.

What you receive

  • A structure register by distance band and chainage
  • A 500 m segment rating along the line
  • Fresh excavation and third-party works flagged between surveys
  • New tracks and access routes across the corridor
  • A change notice after each scheduled re-survey
  • A PDF report and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

Pipelines in mining country

New pits and washing sites near a buried line

Where a pipeline crosses gold-mining districts, galamsey pits, washing sites, spoil and cleared ground can appear within metres of the line, and the streams it crosses can change colour downstream. We map those changes along the corridor and in a band beside it, flag new sites between surveys, and rank the segments where the ground has changed most.

Detection of pits and spoil is tuned and checked on part of your route before it runs on the rest, and each flagged site is confirmed by a reviewer.

The ground, not the people

The register describes land: a pit, a spoil heap, a washing site, cleared ground, and the date it first appears. It never identifies or counts people. What the pipeline owner does with the record, and whom it is shared with, is its decision.

New pipelines

Route options and a baseline before the investment decision

For a pipeline that is still on the drawing board, we compare alignments side by side: the structures within set distances of each option, where built-up land has grown over the past years, and the stretches that cross steep, erosion-prone, low-lying or river-crossing ground. That lets land impact be weighed alongside engineering before the route is fixed.

Once a route is chosen, a dated structure register along it becomes the baseline for acquisition and compensation, and later re-surveys show what appeared after the baseline date.

Under the Environmental Assessment Regulations 2025 (L.I. 2504), onshore petroleum surveys, the construction and operation of onshore pipelines, their maintenance and rehabilitation, and oil and gas pipelines generally are among the undertakings that need an environmental permit. The baseline includes a location map showing communities, water bodies, forest reserves and sacred groves, and we supply those layers to the consultants who prepare the report.

Plants, stations and depots

Perimeters, safety zones and sensitive sites

Perimeter change

New structures, cleared ground and tracks at the fence lines of processing plants, compressor and booster stations and depots, compared between dated surveys, with fences and gates checked by a reviewer on drone imagery.

Structures in your safety zones

You supply the zones from your safety studies or emergency plans; we list each structure inside them with its distance to the source, and show how the count changes between surveys.

Satellite at listed facilities

Some energy installations are listed drone no-fly facilities, so we use satellite imagery there. Your own facilities are never recorded as encroachment.

Upstream and downstream work

Permits and contracts on petroleum projects

Service companies working for upstream operators need a permit from the Petroleum Commission before operations start (Petroleum Commission). The application asks for company, tax and social-security documents and certificates from professional bodies, and the Commission lists the petroleum local-content regulations, L.I. 2204 as amended by L.I. 2435, among the rules it applies. For upstream work, the proposal states how the permit requirement is met and which company contracts with you.

Drone flights along a pipeline follow the GCAA’s rules: no flight within 30 m of buildings, vehicles or groups of people without explicit permission, no flight near listed facilities without prior approval and security clearance, and an operator whose certificate covers the work. That is why corridor work starts from satellite.

How it works

From route file to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the route and the corridor width, and tell us what the register is for: routine right-of-way management, a new route, a handover or a compensation process.

  2. Screen

    Dated satellite scenes, open building datasets and imagery you already hold give the first register along the whole line, with no one on site.

  3. Review

    A person checks what the models propose, adds what they missed and lists what the imagery cannot settle for a field check.

  4. Detail and repeat

    Drone checks of flagged stretches where the approvals allow, then scheduled re-surveys with a change notice after each one.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map structures, fresh digging, spoil, cleared ground and tracks visible from the air
  • Measure each structure to the centreline and group it by band and segment
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Compare route options before a line is built

What we don’t do

  • Detect leaks, taps or the condition of the pipe
  • Identify, count or follow people, or provide security
  • Decide whether a structure is authorised, or verify title
  • Replace patrols, field checks or the census

Frequently asked questions

Does this replace pipeline patrols?

No. It tells patrols where the ground has changed since the last survey, and which 500 m segments to visit first. The register goes with them, so what they find on the ground can be added to the same record.

Which corridor width do you measure?

The one in your acquisition instrument, wayleave or company standard, measured either side of the centreline you send, or from the corridor boundary if you send it as a polygon. A Supreme Court judgment of December 2021 describes one onshore gas corridor as “a 35 metre corridor”, which is 17.5 m either side of the line. Wider reporting bands, such as 50, 100 and 200 m, can be added.

Can you detect leaks, taps or damage to the pipe?

No. Imagery cannot see a leak, a tap or the condition of a buried pipe. We map what is visible at the surface, such as new structures, fresh digging, spoil, trenches, new tracks and cleared ground, and flag it for your teams to check.

Can you cover gas processing plants, depots and the refinery?

From satellite imagery, yes. The GCAA’s no-fly circular lists the oil refinery, a gas processing plant, power stations and ports among the facilities drones may not approach without prior approval and security clearance, so work around them starts from satellite scenes. Any drone flight near an energy installation is planned with the owner’s written consent and the approvals the site needs.

Do you need a Petroleum Commission permit to work for us?

Service companies working in upstream petroleum need a Petroleum Commission permit before operations start. For an upstream contract, the proposal states how the permit requirement is met, and which company holds the contract.

Can you help compare routes for a new pipeline?

Yes. We count the structures within set distances of each alignment, show where settlement is growing near each one, and flag steep, flood-prone and river-crossing stretches, so land impact can be weighed before the route is fixed. The same layers feed the baseline an environmental permit application needs.

Send your pipeline route

Send the centreline or the corridor polygon (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage), the regions and districts it crosses, the corridor width in your acquisition instrument or wayleave, and the date the record must reflect. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
